newsitem.title: FRANCE: INSTANT VIEW - French Prime Minister Jospin speech.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - French Prime Minister Jospin speech.

text.p: Following are immediate comments by financial market analysts on Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's debut policy speech to the French National Assembly on Thursday.
PHILIPPE BROSSARD, HEAD OF RESEARCH, ABN AMRO FINANCE

A couple of surprises. First the minimum wage is going to be increased by less than expected which means the Socialists have not given much to the Communists (who were seeking a eight percent increase)
It shows policy remains slow and cautious..it shows they want to achieve things over a five year period.
Another surprise is that they have got a long catalogue of expension measures ... it seems Jospin has commited himself a bit more today. We still have the question of how they will fund this.
I think the French market is still under pressure...the market may still have a bit more to come down.
PAUL HORNE, ECONOMIST, SMITH BARNEY
I think the prime minister was very consistent with the programme his party had put forward, the main emphasis being on sitmulating the economy with increased revenue for consumers.
BOND FUTURES TRADER, FRENCH BANK

Nothing stuck out for me particularly. I said this morning there was no way, whatever he said, it would be bond friendly, but it's not terribly specific...reducing the working week, making it harder for firms to fire people...none of these measures will make it easier to reduce the government borrowing requirement.
DAVID NAUDE, ECONOMIST, JP MORGAN:
Overall I think it was pretty cautious. There were some good surprises and some, expected messages which could be negative for the market.

The minimum wage rise was in line with our expectations. It should be seen as reasonable and shows the strength of the prime minister vis-a-vis the Communists. It sets the tone for the wages conference -- one of reasonable increases in wages.
Another positive measure is that the mini-budget is off until September. It means they are taking their time.
(On absence of reference to Maastricht deficit goals), I think he (Jospin) was constrained by the audit of public finances, not being able to say more at this stage.
He held to his view that there needs to be growth on the way to European monetary union but did not question the single currency itself.
A lot of things he announced are things the market does not care about, such as justice reform, but they are important.

On privatisations, it is interesting that he makes the distinction between the public service and the public sector. It was a balanced statement. I would not read this as saying France Telecom is not going to be privatised.
I don't expect him to abandon the reform of health spending.
